questions.question: What is a template-driven Angular form, and how do `FormsModule`, `NgForm`, and `NgModel` work together?
questions.title: Template-driven Angular Forms
questions.direct_answer: A template-driven form declares fields and validation mainly in HTML. `FormsModule` provides the form directives, `NgForm` represents the form and collects its controls, and each named `NgModel` connects an input to component data while registering control value and state with the form.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Import `FormsModule` in the standalone component that owns the form template.
`NgForm` represents the form's values, validity, submission state, and controls.
`NgModel` connects a form control to a component property.
A control inside `NgForm` needs a `name` so Angular can register it.
`(ngSubmit)` handles form submission through Angular without a page reload.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A template-driven form is an Angular form whose control structure and validation rules are declared mainly in the HTML template. It is designed for small or straightforward forms where two-way binding and familiar form markup keep the implementation readable.

`FormsModule` makes directives such as `NgForm` and `NgModel` available. When it is imported, Angular places `NgForm` on a normal `form` element and uses it as the parent form controller. A field with `[(ngModel)]` reads its initial value from the component and writes user changes back. Its `name` registers the control under that key, so `NgForm` can build the form value and calculate overall validity.

For example:

```typescript
@Component({
  imports: [FormsModule],
  template: `<form #form="ngForm" (ngSubmit)="save(form)">
    <input name="email" [(ngModel)]="profile.email" required>
    <button [disabled]="form.invalid">Save</button>
  </form>`,
})
class ProfileForm { profile = { email: '' }; save(form: NgForm) {} }
```

The component can inspect `form.value`, `form.valid`, and `form.submitted` in the submit method. A common mistake is omitting `name` inside a form, which prevents normal registration. Template-driven forms are convenient, but their model is assembled through directives and updates asynchronously, so complex cross-field logic, dynamic controls, and detailed unit tests are often clearer with reactive forms. The choice depends on form behaviour, not just field count.

sections.title: Control registration and form state
sections.content:
The browser provides the form elements, while Angular adds a form model around them. Importing `FormsModule` lets Angular recognise `form`, `ngModel`, and validation attributes. `NgForm` becomes the top-level controller and can be exported to a template variable with `#form="ngForm"`.

Each named `NgModel` creates a control and registers it with the nearest parent form. The registration name becomes the key in the form's value object. The directive also tracks whether the field is valid, dirty, touched, or pending. Two-way binding keeps the component property and visible input value connected, although one-way `[ngModel]` and `(ngModelChange)` can express the directions separately.

In a profile form, the email input registers under `email`. Typing changes the model and control state. On submit, `ngSubmit` calls the component method with the current `NgForm`. The button may use overall validity, while an error message can use the exported email control's state.

Template-driven does not remove server validation. Browser code can be bypassed, and rules such as unique email ownership usually require the server. It also becomes hard to follow when controls are created dynamically or many fields depend on one another. In those cases, an explicit reactive form model provides a clearer boundary.

sections.title: Template-driven form registration and submission
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Module[FormsModule imported] --> Form[NgForm on form element]
  Field[Named input with NgModel] --> Register[Control registers with NgForm]
  Model[Component property] <-->|two-way binding| Field
  Register --> State[Form value and validity]
  State --> Submit[ngSubmit handler]
```

questions.question: How do you validate a template-driven Angular form and show useful errors?
questions.title: Template-driven Form Validation
questions.direct_answer: Place supported validation attributes or directive validators on named `NgModel` controls, export each control to read its errors and interaction state, and show a specific message when it is invalid after being touched, made dirty, or submitted. The server must validate the data again.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Attributes such as `required` and `minlength` attach Angular validators.
Show a correction message only after useful user interaction or submission.
Use a separate message for each validation rule that can fail.
Client validation improves feedback; server validation protects the data boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
Validator results, interaction state, and error timing
sections.content:
A validator receives a control value and returns either no error or an object naming the failure. Angular combines all attached validators into the control's status. `NgForm` then combines its registered child statuses, so one invalid required field makes the form invalid.

Status alone does not decide when an error should appear. `dirty` means the value changed through the UI; `touched` means the control lost focus; `submitted` means a submit attempt occurred. A common policy is to show field errors after touched or after submit. This avoids an alarming page full of red messages on the first render while still helping a keyboard user who leaves an empty field.

For a required two-character name, an empty value produces the required error. A one-character value removes that error but produces minlength. Separate messages reflect the current cause. The message element should have an ID referenced by the input, and `aria-invalid` can reflect the visible invalid state.

Some rules cannot be decided locally. Username availability, permissions, and current inventory require a server result. Async or cross-field rules can be implemented in Angular, but reactive forms often make those flows easier to test. In every style, validation must produce a clear correction path and the server remains authoritative.

sections.title: Validation state and message visibility
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Value[Current field value] --> Validators[Required and minlength validators]
  Validators -->|no errors| Valid[Control valid]
  Validators -->|error object| Invalid[Control invalid]
  Invalid --> Interaction{Touched or form submitted?}
  Interaction -->|no| Wait[Message hidden]
  Interaction -->|yes| Message[Specific correction message]
  Valid --> Submit[Form may submit]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between template-driven and reactive forms in Angular?
questions.title: Template-driven and Reactive Forms
questions.direct_answer: Template-driven forms build an implicit form model from template directives and suit smaller forms. Reactive forms create the control model explicitly in TypeScript, expose synchronous control state, and better support complex validation, dynamic structure, and focused tests. Both produce Angular form controls and still need server validation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Template-driven forms define most structure with `NgModel` in the template.
Reactive forms define controls explicitly in TypeScript.
Template-driven forms are concise for small, stable forms.
Reactive forms suit dynamic fields, cross-field rules, and detailed tests.
The two approaches share validation ideas but should not manage one field together.

sections.title: Interview answer
Implicit and explicit form models
sections.content:
Both approaches eventually work with Angular controls, but they create them from opposite directions. Template-driven directives inspect the rendered template and build the model for the component. Reactive code builds the model first, and form directives connect the template to it. This difference affects when the model is available and where a developer looks to understand the form.

A newsletter form with email and consent can stay template-driven: the fields are stable, validation is local, and the markup is easy to read. An order editor with a variable list of items, cross-field totals, and conditional addresses benefits from `FormArray` and explicit validators because the structure itself is application logic.

Reactive forms use immutable state snapshots at the model boundary and provide synchronous access to controls. Template-driven forms rely on directive-driven, asynchronous model updates and usually mutate the bound data object. These characteristics influence testing and complex coordination; they do not make one style automatically faster or more correct.

Mixing `ngModel` and reactive directives on the same control creates two owners and should be avoided. A project can still use template-driven forms on simple screens and reactive forms on complex ones. The choice belongs to each form's behaviour and maintenance needs, while accessible labels, useful errors, submission handling, and server validation are required in both.

sections.title: Form model ownership and best fit
sections.content:
| Concern | Template-driven | Reactive |
|---|---|---|
| Model creation | inferred from template directives | explicit in TypeScript |
| Typical binding | `NgModel` | `formControl` or `formGroup` |
| Strong fit | small, stable forms | dynamic or coordinated forms |
| Unit testing | often includes template directives | form model can be tested directly |
| Main cost | logic can be spread across markup | more setup code |
